blocks.text: "Party Central," a one-stop political buffet that brought together more than 2,500 registered Democrats across the state for a daylong meeting of the party.
And yes, there was a big ballot: "Vote Early, Vote Often" was the Democratic Party's most important message for the caucus season.

Iowa's caucus delegates would be chosen in the precinct caucuses, but the party is going to go all the way to the Republican delegates as well, by nominating delegates for both parties, with two delegates going to each party.
The Democratic delegates will be chosen for caucuses in the 75 counties as well as all of the city and town primaries.
So all the Democrats in the state gathered in Des Moines to make their choice for delegates, which will be announced at the state convention in August.
The results showed what a dominant presence the Des Moines County Democratic Party has in the state.
It had 85 of the 122 delegates, a significant advantage over the second largest party, Polk County, with 16.

More than 900 Iowa Democrats were invited to the event, which included 22 different sessions on everything from politics to the environment to health care, as well as party contests on a host of issues, including gun control, taxes and immigration.
(Most of those are open issues in Iowa, with a few party contests reserved for the Republican caucus only.)
The "Party Central" event is the first of three big party events before the Iowa caucuses.
On Monday, May 5, in Iowa City, the Democratic and Republican parties are scheduled to co-sponsor a big forum on the Iowa caucuses in the Iowa City Opera House.

Last month, an earthquake measuring 6.5 on the Richter scale struck in the remote Gobi Desert in southern Mongolia, just four days after Paul's departure.

The quake brought panic and fear to an already fragile homeland of the country's 3 million people – with the World Health Organisation reporting nearly 200 casualties including the death of a young mother and her infant daughter.
The situation in Mongolia today has led New Zealand's Minister for Women's Affairs, Megan Woods, to travel to Mongolia as part of an emergency deployment.

She will be working alongside United Nations representatives, international partners, non-governmental organisations and local government to provide humanitarian aid and assistance to earthquake victims.
New Zealanders have a good track record in providing humanitarian assistance in crisis situations, and we have been a big contributor to the UN humanitarian system.
In this case, we have committed $13.4 million – which covers the cost of an initial relief package – and have committed an additional $12 million to the UN Central Emergency Response Fund.
This comes on top of our recent contribution of $1 million in emergency funding for the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The assistance and support provided by New Zealand comes during a difficult time in Mongolia.
